Watch: Philp and Yusuf have public clash over immigration

Published 13 November 2026

Conservative MP Chris Philp and Reform UK's Zia Yusuf had a blazing row at a joint press conference, as they joined villagers protesting against asylum accommodation plans.

The pair clashed when sharing a platform in Piddington to oppose converting a former military site at MoD Bicester into accommodation for more than 1,200 detained asylum seekers.

The two politicians were invited to make speeches about the plans, but things became heated after Yusuf asked Philp to apologise for the Conservatives' record on immigration.

Philp, the shadow home secretary, told Yusuf to "calm down" and accused him of "cheap politics", an assertion Reform's home affairs spokesman dismissed.

Asylum centre on military base near Piddington approved Published 1 day ago

A press conference led by Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally took place on Friday after Housing Secretary Angela Rayner approved the Home Office's application to change the use of the site for asylum accommodation.

The Home Office said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken.

There has been significant local opposition to the proposal and a legal challenge to the planning decision is expected from the parish council.

In September, Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the planned use for the site in Oxfordshire.

Politicians from the Conservatives and Reform have made several visits to Piddington, a village of about 350 people, to show their support for campaigners.

Speaking on Friday, Philp said a future Conservative government would shut the asylum accommodation "straight away" if it was opened by Labour.

Yusuf made clear Reform's opposition to the plans before his focus switched to the Conservatives.

He said: "It's obviously true that we would not be gathered here today and 1,200 men would not be being dumped into this beautiful village were it not for the actions of the Conservative government.

"So I actually want to ask you Chris, would you actually like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into this country illegally?"

Philp, a former immigration minister, described Yusuf's remarks as "disingenuous" and argued the migrants who could be housed near Piddington will have arrived in the country while Labour has been in power.

He said the Conservatives are under new leadership and he hoped the politicians could "stand in solidarity with the residents" rather than "engage in point scoring".

Philp added: "Zia, read the room, listen to the people clapping and read the room."

Yusuf countered that it was "important that we hold everybody accountable for this situation" and said Philp had been "heavily involved in immigration and borders policy" for the Conservatives in government.

Philp repeated his "read the room" suggestion, adding: "The public here want you to pipe down on the cheap politics."

Yusuf dismissed the suggestion that he was engaging in "cheap politics" and repeated his criticism of the Conservatives' record, saying they "refused" to secure the country's borders when in power.

As Yusuf spoke, Philp could be heard saying: "Buddy, I'm not here to give you comms advice, mate, you're in a hole stop digging."

Philp told Yusuf he should "calm down", with the Reform politician repeating his request for the Conservative MP to "apologise to the British people".

McNally thanked the pair for attending the press conference, adding: "I understand this is a passionate discussion and I respect you both for what you've got to do and what you represent."

While the two parties are on the right of politics, it is unusual for them to share a platform to campaign and both are keen to stress their differences to voters.

Reform leader Nigel Farage has pitched the party as replacing the "old, fuddy-duddy" Conservatives , and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform to secure power.

Up to 1,256 men could be housed at the site near Bicester under the plans

Government ministers want to use former military bases as part of efforts close all asylum hotels.

Insisting that the MoD Bicester accommodation will be safe, the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said such sites are "designed to be self-contained with 24/7 security and CCTV to minimise the impact on the local community".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also previously said it should not just be the poorest communities receiving dispersed refugees and asylum seekers.

Liberal Democrat MP Calum Miller told the BBC he was "very disappointed" but not "surprised" by the government's decision to grant planning permission.

Miller, whose constituency of Bicester and Woodstock includes the military site, said "the government was marking the government's application".

He said the decision "lays bare the weakness of the application and the many, many problems with it, because this is not a suitable site and it is not the right place to put a large-scale asylum centre".

stories.body:
In today’s newsletter: US intelligence reportedly believes the former tech executive was recruited by Beijing, raising questions about the security of the AI industry and Trump’s close ties to Nvidia chief Jensen Huang

Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang , the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies.

Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines.

Five big stories

UK | Ministers are considering changing the law to force the entertainment industry to better protect women and children in the wake of the revelations over David Walliams and the conviction of Russell Brand.

Climate | The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.

US midterms | Democrat Scott Colom has become the first Black senator in Mississippi to be elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.

Europe | Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years , setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.

Technology | Police officers risk arresting innocent people , especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.

In depth: Everything we know (or don’t) about the Nvidia affair

Last month, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, the former executive of a Singapore-based computing company, Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia; it buys the extremely valuable chips they produce, which are essential for powering AI, and rents computing space to Chinese companies. The US government had already been investigating whether Megaspeed could be flouting US restrictions and smuggling chips into China – allegations that both Nvidia and Megaspeed deny.

US intelligence officials, who had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, eventually concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who had been passing on information to Beijing. The intelligence behind this assessment is classified, so we don’t know exactly what they found – or which intelligence body was conducting the surveillance. Nvidia said Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected”, but on Sunday, Huang admitted in a letter to his employees that he had been having an affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children,” he said, adding that he was “deeply sorry”.

Nvidia’s valuation is inextricably linked to Huang. By yesterday, $430bn (5.5%) had been wiped off its share price, and in the early hours of this morning, that figure ballooned to about $600bn following reports that Nvidia’s board was deciding whether to oust Huang (you can follow the latest on that here ). The company has appointed outside counsel to review the pair’s relationship and says it has no reason to believe that secrets or national security were compromised.

The most interesting aspects of this story are the questions we can’t (yet) answer. Did Nvidia’s board know that US intelligence suspected Alice Huang was a spy? What evidence led US intelligence to conclude she was spying for China ? What information could she have passed to Beijing? And …

Who is Alice Huang?

Reporters and sleuths on Chinese social media have been trying to get to the bottom of who the Megaspeed chief really is. On Tuesday, the Financial Times published an interesting report (£) about Alice Huang’s backstory. She was born in the rural area of Hunan, worked as a journalist at China’s state broadcaster, then at HSBC and the investment bank Citic Securities. In 2015, she joined an investment management company Hexi.

There, she met financier Kang Wei. The two became romantically involved, and together they reinvented themselves as AI entrepreneurs. In 2023, Huang and her business partners acquired Megaspeed, a Singaporean subsidiary of a Chinese gaming company, which she and Wei aimed to turn into a datacentre business. According to the FT’s report, the two pitched investors on their ability to secure access to Nvidia chips.

Nobody knows exactly when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, when their relationship became romantic, or what information she might have passed to Beijing while it was going on. The earliest picture of them together is at an after-party following a tech trade show in Taipei, taken in 2024. As Aisha Down and Dan Milmo pointed out earlier this week, Jensen Huang is close to Donald Trump, so it’s possible that Alice Huang could have gained glimpses into US AI policy as it was being formed, into Trump’s thinking on AI, or into Nvidia’s company strategy. But without seeing the evidence, all this is speculation.

What does this reveal about Chinese espionage?

The US has been historically cautious about allowing AI chips to end up in Chinese hands. In 2022, Joe Biden’s administration introduced the Chips and Science Act, which restricted the sale of US chips in China, banning the export of most Nvidia chips. “The Chinese have a very strong pedigree for industrial espionage and copying other nations’ technologies,” Steve Tsang, the director of the SOAS China Institute, tells me. “They’ve been doing this for decades. And now it’s no longer engines they’re interested in, but AI.”

Both the US and China have an interest in gathering intelligence about each other’s AI firms. What’s more remarkable is the possibility that the Chinese spy agency, the MSS, could have recruited Alice Huang as a “honeytrap” to ensnare Jensen Huang – a method fraught with risk, which seems more reminiscent of 1970s spy fiction than contemporary counterintelligence (China, for its part, has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a spy).

“The facts clearly aren’t established, but it seems more likely that if Alice Huang was working for Beijing, the MSS would have recruited her after they became aware of her relationship with Huang, not before,” Nigel Inkster, the former director of operations and intelligence for the British Secret Intelligence Service, tells me.

China has built a large intelligence gathering operation: the MSS is now bigger than the CIA, and various national security laws mean that Chinese nationals can be required to provide assistance to the Chinese state. “You have a lot of people who can be co-opted into intelligence gathering, all of whom can be tasked with different requirements,” Inkster says. “Business delegations travelling abroad can be tasked with gathering information. So can visiting academics.”

“The big question, to my mind, is whether the Chinese intelligence agencies have actually been willing to deliver unwelcome information to the party leadership,” Inkster adds.

What approach has the US taken?

Jensen Huang is the most influential figure in the US AI industry outside major labs such as Anthropic, and has cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump . He’s successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen regulations on AI and roll back restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China (last year, Trump controversially approved the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chips directly to China in exchange for the federal government taking a 25% cut). Huang was present at the White House twice last month: once for a state dinner with Xi Jinping, and again for a meeting of tech and AI executives.

Huang’s close relationship with Trump could help explain why the president has so far played down concerns about Chinese espionage, appearing remarkably ambivalent about the recent allegations. The president was reportedly briefed last year about US intelligence conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, and in spring this year, his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, supervised the drafting of a classified memo warning that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with a Chinese spy. In May, Trump issued a last-minute invitation to Jensen Huang to board Air Force One in Alaska and join a delegation of executives bound to China. A US government official told reporters at the New York Times that when Rubio learned that Huang would be joining the trip in Alaska, he briefed Trump on the memo.

But on Monday, Trump, who is due to meet Xi Jinping later this month, said he had not known at the time of the trip about Huang’s relationship. He said the FBI had been investigating a matter relating to Huang, and defended the Nvidia CEO, describing him as an “honourable guy” who “built a great American company”.

What else we’ve been reading

I loved Arifa Akbar’s story on theatregoers donning costumes to watch their favourite shows, though I’m not entirely convinced that wearing feline ears to watch Cats absolves her from “veering into fandom” … Michael

Joanna Moorhead uncovers the growing disquiet surrounding a little known collection of Indigenous artefacts handed over to powerful Catholic missionaries and now held at the Vatican Museums in Rome. Libby

Martin Lewis writes about his Small Ideas Initiative – quick fixes to make Britain work better, suggested by the public – with infectious enthusiasm. I just hope the government reads to the bit where he reminds us small fixes have to work alongside bigger structural change. Libby

Providence, Rhode Island, has become the second US city to divest Israel (Somerville, Massachusetts was first) in a landslide vote. Claire Wang has the details . Michael

Wire in, as they say in Scotland: our Comfort Eating podcast is back with a new host , the magnificent Siobhán McSweeney. Libby

Football | Harry Kane says he still feels a pressure to prove his worth, even as he prepares to become England’s most capped men’s player, as he outlined his determination to set records that will stand for years.

Cricket | White-ball tour begins in Perth on Friday , but there is only one story in Australian cricket and the tourists are not it.

Fifa | A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for an investigation into claims an individual on the Fifa payroll was working privately as a housekeeper for Gianni Infantino.

The front pages

“TV industry must tackle abuse or face crackdown, ministers warn”, is the Guardian ’s splash today. Metro writes “Another mystery star bids to block claims”.

The Times writes “Milburn: Cut sick benefits to force young into work”, and the i Paper has “Under-25s with ADHD won’t get £217-a-month benefits in new welfare reforms”.

The FT leads with “Democrats pledge to expose ‘absolute avalanche of corruption’ under Trump”, the Mail has “Even Cameron tells PM: Don’t rejoin the EU”, and the Telegraph writes “SAS issues warning over troop witch hunts”. The Mirror says “Not even a bed for an OAP with cancer”, and the Express has “‘Sanctuary in nature helped me to recover’”.

The Latest

Trump’s $10bn BBC battle: judge rules lawsuit can go ahead

Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC has been granted permission to proceed, after the corporation’s attempt to get it dismissed was thrown out by a Trump-appointed Florida judge. The case focuses on an edit in a 2024 Panorama documentary that spliced two comments together that were made by the president during a rally before the January 6 Capitol riots, for which the BBC has apologised. With the lawsuit now set to continue, what’s at stake for press freedom? Lucy Hough speaks to global editor, Devika Bhat .

Cartoon of the day | Nicola Jennings

The Upside

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Researchers from the Hoag Family Cancer Institute have made a potential breakthrough in the early diagnosis of ovarian cancer – a disease often detected after it has spread.

For decades, efforts to detect the cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumours. “We asked … what if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” said study leader Rajan Gogna.

Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. The study found that women experiencing these changes have elevated levels of a molecule called Tu-Stroma in their blood.

The study’s co-author Dr Esha Madan says the discovery “could transform how we approach prevention”.

Decision disappoints experts hoping for world’s biggest emitter to take global lead on climate crisis

China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.

The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate .

Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”

China is in the midst of an economic transformation , from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.

Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.

Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year .

The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.

Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.

“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.

“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”

It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.

After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor , the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.

The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.

after newsletter promotion

China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues , setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.

Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C.

That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “ overshoot ”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.

India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.

The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand.

No decision on a host is likely to be made at this year’s Cop31 meeting , which is ongoing in Turkey, with the Turkish and Australian governments jointly presiding over the summit.

stories.body:
Huw Irranca-Davies became the Senedd's presiding officer following the May election

Published 13 November 2026

A senior Reform politician says a no-confidence vote in the Senedd's presiding officer is "not off the table", after a party member was banned for claiming white people were being "replaced".

Llŷr Powell, Reform's chief whip in Cardiff Bay, said his colleague Joe Martin had the right to raise "legitimate concerns" that were being "infringed upon".

Martin was told he would not be called to speak in the Welsh Parliament until he apologised for the remarks made on Tuesday, which Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies called "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".

Reform withdrew from most Senedd proceedings on Wednesday in response.

Powell, who as chief whip enforces party discipline in the Senedd's Reform group, was asked on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast if his party would put forward a no confidence vote in Irranca-Davies.

He said: "I'm not going to say that we're going to do that now, but what I would say is it's not off the table right now because freedom of speech and the right of members to raise legitimate concerns should be the main priority.

"And for us, right now, we see that as being infringed upon."

Powell denied Martin had made any connection to a far-right conspiracy theory that the white population was being deliberately replaced by the immigration of other ethnic groups.

"Joe was asking a legitimate question based on demographic changes," Powell said.

"The idea that he was framing some far-right theory is false.

"He was talking about legitimate concerns that is out there for data for all to see."

Reform's Joe Martin, party leader Helen Jenner and chief whip Llŷr Powell announced the boycott on the Senedd's steps on Wednesday

During business questions on Tuesday, Martin had asked Welsh government minister Heledd Fychan for a "statement from your government on the demographic replacement of white British people taking place in the UK".

"Mass immigration and differing birth rates mean that, in just 37 years' time, in 2063, we will be a minority in our own country," he said.

Fychan had asked the deputy presiding officer, who had been chairing the session, whether the question broke Senedd rules.

Irranca-Davies later called Martin's statement "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive" and "clearly discriminatory" when he issued the speaking ban.

He said that unless Martin apologised to the Senedd chamber "we will not be calling him to speak".

Aliya Mohammed, chief executive of the charity Race Equality First, criticised Martin on Wednesday, saying "the idea that white people are being 'replaced' is linked to a conspiracy theory that creates division and wrongly portrays people from minority ethnic backgrounds as a threat".

Martin, a Member of the Senedd (MS) representing Caerdydd Penarth, was accused by Plaid Cymru of dangerous rhetoric in June when he claimed attacks from Sudanese asylum seekers were inevitable .

The next day MSs walked out during a speech where Martin joked that Welsh students were unable to read, and Indian nurses were taking Welsh jobs .

He was later accused by the presiding officer of making offensive remarks in a debate about the crisis-hit Welsh Gender Service .

stories.title: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds - but are they value for money?
stories.summary: Beauty calendars have become a Christmas staple and have become particularly popular with female shoppers.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 6 hours ago

It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach.

"I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering.

Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar.

Customers likened the contents of Kim Kardashian's Skims calendar to something you would find down the back of a sofa

This week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa.

Julia says she earns a good salary but is keen to get value for money and doesn't want to waste it on items she won't use.

"I spent £160 on a Space NK fragrance calendar last year," she says. "I got some fragrances I'd been wanting for a while for a lot less than recommended retail price, and those I didn't like I managed to sell on for a slight mark-up on what I paid."

Julia, 39, says she thinks fragrance calendars are usually good value for money

Beauty calendars, which often cost upwards of £100 and sometimes much more, have been around for more than a decade and the marketing has grown ever more sophisticated.

High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight.

And it appears to be working. Ipsos data shows , external around 15% of all advent calendars sold are beauty ones, with people aged 18-34 particularly willing to splash out.

But in the face of that tsunami of marketing, customers seem to be getting savvier.

"I love beauty, but I rarely buy beauty advent calendars. They are pricey and often only have a few things that I actually want to try or are trending products," says Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist.

She thinks some are good value but, for her, the advantage is being able to try on a small scale without forking out for a full-size product.

"For me, an advent calendar - particularly a beauty one - serves the purpose of allowing me to try out different products, particularly in the lead-up to Christmas, and then I can hopefully snag a bargain in the Boxing Day sales."

Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist, says the calendars "serve the purpose of allowing me to try out different products"

Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, also likes the general idea, but has a healthy scepticism around a lot of them in practice.

"I do think some brands take the consumer for granted in that they provide each day with something so menial that people are bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items.

"And when that's the case, they certainly put me off as the excitement to open each window dwindles into irritation rather than joy."

Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, is less keen on the calendars and says they leave consumers "bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items"

Jessica Jasper, a marketing consultant, is more positive - she thinks it's worth it. But she also thinks some companies are just jumping on a trend and that "some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing".

So can beauty calendars offer value for both the brands and the customer - an example of a win-win? Or are they mainly designed to make us spend more at Christmas than we need to?

"Some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing," says marketing consultant Jessica Jasper

Heather Widdows, a philosophy professor and beauty expert, has pointed out that while you might buy some of the products in an advent calendar individually, it's highly unlikely you'd buy all of them.

"Beauty calendars may offer you lots of products for a really good price. They can also be a bit of fun and feel sensuous.

"But it is exceptionally unlikely that you would use all the products inside them, so they're probably not worth it."

This year, Julia has spent £99 on a John Lewis fragrance calendar which she thinks is good value for money. But it doesn't mean she'll keep everything in it.

In fact she's joined a Facebook group where people trade the ones they don't want for ones they do.

"The ones I keep are already a lot cheaper per mililitre than if you bought them at retail," she says.

stories.title: SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch
stories.summary: It felt like stepping into the future.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
It felt like stepping into the future.

STARBASE, Texas —The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.

Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.

Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.

We are dazzled

This was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different, difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.

Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power, and be captured by the tower.

It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before, by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks.

Nevertheless, it happened.

Rapid reuse is firmly on the horizon

Humans have built reusable spacecraft that flew into orbit before. In the 1970s, flush with confidence after the triumphant Moon landings, NASA designed and built several Space Shuttles. They had solid rocket boosters that were fished from the ocean and reused. The large orange external tank was not recovered after each flight, but the orbiters went to space for two weeks, or even longer, before returning to Earth and landing on a runway.

The shuttles were engineering marvels. But during the return to Earth they acted as gliders, not igniting their engines. And their heat shields were delicate flowers, requiring painstaking refurbishment after each flight. At the outset of the shuttle program, the space agency contemplated sending dozens of humans into space at a time, and carrying cargo at a cost as low of $25 per pound.

Reality never matched these rosy projections. The crew space capped out at seven astronauts, and the cost-per-pound was closer to $25,000. Each orbiter cost an extraordinary amount of money to build; NASA only ever built five that went to space.

SpaceX has five Starships in an advanced state of development at Starbase today; and its factory houses the components for a dozen more. The company can currently manufacture a Starship upper stage in its South Texas Starfactory every three weeks. The factory was sized to produce a ship every three days. When SpaceX founder Elon Musk discussed these build targets in an interview five years ago, he sounded mad. But he no longer does.

A proof of concept

The Space Shuttle was nearly a fully reusable space launch system, but it fell far short of low-cost, rapid launch. Over 30 years the vehicle made 135 flights. Within a few years SpaceX aims to fly 135 times a year, then thousands of times.

Such was the significance of Saturday. SpaceX aspires to fundamentally change the relationship between humanity and the heavens. The first step is to get the entire rocket back. SpaceX has now returned both elements of a Starship rocket safely to its launch tower. It will take time to reach a high rate of success with such landings, but Saturday’s safe return offered a proof of concept.

The landings will come with increasing frequency; and so will the launches. Over time SpaceX will perfect the heat shield that is likely to be the most difficult aspect of rapid reuse. And eventually, as difficult as it may be to believe, what we experienced with amazement this weekend will become routine. One day, we will take this all for granted.

But not today.

stories.body:
Despite John Healey’s defiance, the economy faces threats from a tech slowdown and energy bills this winter

AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years

The forecasters were clear when John Healey became chancellor in July: Britain’s resilience to the war in the Middle East would not last. The global economic headwinds were too strong, inflation was beginning to rise and growth would slow to a trickle.

Four months into the job, the economy is continuing to defy expectations after growing by 0.7% in the third quarter – the fastest expansion in two and a half years. It puts the UK on course to be the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year.

On his first day in Downing Street the memo from the Treasury showed the most optimistic City analyst expected 0.3% quarterly growth. Most had pencilled in a figure close to zero. Some were warning that the UK could edge towards a recession.

Despite the gloomy outlook households have continued to spend and business investment has powered ahead, driven by the rollout of AI.

Underneath the bonnet, growth is being spearheaded by IT and professional services – together contributing about half of the rise in activity. As the central sectors in the AI boom, that is hardly surprising – with analysts at ING suggesting the strength in IT was “very clearly a datacentre story” thanks to the UK’s status as a leading destination in Europe for investment.

Overall, Deutsche Bank estimates that AI-related spending has added about 0.3% to 0.4% to GDP growth this year. It is clear to see why Healey is keen to build on the groundwork laid by his immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, to harness AI amid government efforts to court global business investment.

Meanwhile, household consumption is up by 1.6% so far this year – helped by spending over the warm summer months even as consumers faced a living standards squeeze because the Iran war fuelled a surge in petrol and diesel prices.

However, the fear is that the UK’s initial resilience to the global economic storm emanating from the Middle East will soon fizzle out.

Both of Britain’s recent growth engines face a tougher period ahead.

After the US midterm elections and revelations at the chipmaker Nvidia , the outlook for the AI investment boom is less certain. Financial markets have been rocked in recent weeks amid fears that a bubble in AI stocks could be about to burst . A slowdown in technology investment could hit the UK. Still, the hope is that swelling demand for AI will not evaporate overnight.

after newsletter promotion

For households, however, a tough winter lies ahead. Energy bills are poised to increase by about a quarter in January, with the average annual household gas and electricity bill expected to climb to more than £2,000. Analysts say it is hard to see how consumer spending would not come under greater pressure in the new year.

In the latest data there were some early warning signs: retail sales and consumer discretionary spending fell in September. Real wage growth is cooling and the headline inflation rate is on track to reach a fresh peak of close to 5% next year.

With growth proving resilient, the Bank of England will feel emboldened to raise interest rates to combat imported inflation. City investors expect at least two more quarter-point increases to 4.5% before the end of next year. That will hit the brakes on the economy and add to the cost of living squeeze.

At last month’s budget Healey struck a defiant tone by arguing that the UK could continue to defy forecasters expectations. That task, however, is becoming increasingly tough.

stories.body:
Battery maker CATL aims to have 2,000 swapping stations in China by the end of 2027 and to bring the tech to Europe

E very day, Wang Bing drives his big electric lorry to send about five tonnes of goods between the cities of Haikou and Dongfang on Hainan, a tropical island in southern China . A round trip covers about 500 kilometres (310 miles). But refuelling is not something Wang worries about.

“When my battery runs low, I just drive my truck into a battery-swapping station to get a fully charged one,” says the 53-year-old, who shares the journey with a colleague in eight-hour shifts.

Wang has been a lorry driver for nearly three decades. In the first two of those, he drove conventional lorries fuelled by diesel. About five years ago, he began driving an electric model after the logistics company he worked for upgraded its fleet. In July this year, his old e-truck, which used conventional plug-in charging, was replaced by one with a swappable battery.

In the past, Wang had to spend an hour and half charging his battery each time, but with his new truck, it takes just five minutes or so to have a drained battery removed and a fresh one replaced. “I am very happy,” he says.

Battery swapping is not new in China, where more than 400,000 e-trucks (or over 90% of the global total ) were sold last year. The Chinese carmaker Nio commercialised the technology nearly a decade ago for smaller electric vehicles (EVs). But in 2023, the Chinese battery behemoth CATL launched a battery-swapping system for electric lorries through a subsidiary brand called Qiji Energy.

To Wang, the biggest advantage of the technology is the time it saves. “It is much, much faster,” he says. “I don’t even need to leave my truck when the battery is being swapped.”

This swiftness builds on the cost advantage e-trucks already have over their fossil-fuelled peers when it comes to refuelling.

“Electricity is cheaper than oil,” Wang says. The per-kilometre fuelling cost for an e-truck works out about 1.1 yuan (12p) in Hainan, he says, significantly lower than that for a diesel truck, which exceeds 2 yuan (22p) a kilometre. “That means my e-truck can save more than 20,000 yuan (£2,200) per month,” Wang says.

When a truck approaches a battery-swapping station, the station’s cameras automatically identify the type of battery it uses by checking its number plate. “All the driver needs to do is to drive the truck into a designated area, and the battery will be swapped completely automatically,” says Wei Jiuchun, 46, a test driver at a Qiji Energy battery-swapping station in Suzhou, east China. Wei’s job is to help the station test its system for different models of heavy trucks and under different weather conditions.

It is not just time and fuel costs the technology saves but, in China, the initial lump sum a buyer has to put down to get an e-truck, says Mao Shiyue, a Beijing-based researcher at the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT).

The upfront purchase price for an e-truck is significantly higher than for a comparable diesel model, a major obstacle for those vehicles’ wider adoption in many parts of the world. In China, a customer opting for battery swapping typically buys an e-truck without a battery, and then rents the battery from a service provider. As the cost of a battery is about 40% of an e-truck’s price, the business model can make e-trucks a lot more affordable, Mao says.

The technology can also help minimise the pressure EV charging brings to the power grid, according to Mao, because swapping stations have more flexibility to spread out the charging time for the depleted batteries.

“If the grid sees a spike in electricity demand during peak hours, those stations can even act as an energy-storage station by returning the electricity stored in their batteries back to the grid to ease the strain,” he says.

after newsletter promotion

CATL, the world’s biggest battery manufacturer, is a key player in promoting battery swapping for heavy trucks in China. The company’s support for the technology is critical for its large-scale rollout, says Phate Zhang, the founder of CnEVPost, a Shanghai-based outlet focusing on EVs.

CATL plans to put 900 battery-swapping stations into operation across China by the end of this year, expanding its current network twice more. By the end of 2027, it wants the number to reach 2,000.

The company has also teamed up with the London-based renewable energy supplier Octopus to bring the technology to Europe. It intends to open its first group of battery-swapping “mega hubs” in the UK next year, and a network of more than 30 hubs in Europe by 2035.

In China, battery-swapping is still a minority charging method for its rapidly growing e-truck fleet. In 2024, about one-third of the zero-emission trucks in the country featured this technology, while the rest largely had conventional plug-in charging, according to the latest available figures .

One downside is that drivers often need to stick to a particular service provider that caters to the specific type of swappable batteries their e-trucks use.

“For example, some batteries are swapped from the chassis, while others are swapped from the top of the truck,” says Xue Lulu, a senior associate at World Resources Institute China. “Even under the same technological route, batteries made by different companies often have different specifications.” This means drivers cannot drop into any random swapping station to get their trucks replenished, which could restrict the journeys they can make, she says.

Plus, battery swapping doesn’t necessarily mean drivers will save time, Xue says. During her field research in China, she found some lorry drivers would wait outside battery-swapping stations for one to two hours before going in because they wanted to avoid using the service during peak hours, to save money. “Logistics firms are extremely sensitive to costs,” she says.

The most suitable users are probably drivers who, like Wang, work on fixed routes served by battery-swapping stations. Mao says the charging method has been rolled out most successfully among companies that use heavy trucks in specific settings, such as those carrying goods in ports and factories, as well as within a city or between two nearby cities. “For unpredicted and long-haul routes, there are still challenges for rolling it out on a large scale,” he says.

stories.title: Smart glasses banned from Welsh Parliament after ruling they could be used for speeches
stories.summary: The decision comes while a review of the use of the devices in the Senedd takes place.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Jason O'Connell has used smart glasses to deliver speeches in the Senedd

Published 13 November 2026

The Senedd's presiding officer has in effect banned the use of smart glasses in the Welsh Parliament, days after it emerged he would allow them to be used as a teleprompter.

Huw Irranca-Davies had ruled that using them in such a way was OK - provided he was alerted first - but Members of the Senedd (MS) have now been told he "will not be considering any other requests" to use the devices.

He said that will remain the case until a review into the use of the devices on the Senedd estate ends.

Reform's Jason O'Connell made headlines earlier this year after using the glasses to help him make a speech .

O'Connell, whose glasses do not include a camera, said he had voluntarily agreed not to use his device until the review is complete.

The MS for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr previously said he had started using glasses as a teleprompter to improve his speaking skills and to avoid looking down at his notes.

A letter from Irranca-Davies from 20 October, published in committee papers last week, said he had "determined that members may use smart glasses as a teleprompter in the chamber, provided that they give me advance notice".

Unlike other types of smart glasses that have caused controversy, like the ones above, O'Connell's do not have a camera built into them

On Tuesday, an official working for the presiding officer told MSs that "he will not be considering any other requests to use AI-equipped glasses in the Siambr until the review has reported".

They said: "Following further helpful discussions, no members will be using the technology until the review has been completed."

The official said the next stage of the Senedd Commission's review would include a consultation with MSs and staff, and would be completed by the end of 2026 with recommendations "brought forward in the new year".

O'Connell told BBC Wales after the decision: "I've voluntarily agreed to stop using the ones I'm using as a teleprompter until the review completes."

Asked how he felt about the matter, he said: "I'm ambivalent. They were a useful tool to be used on occasions.

"I was no way reliant on their use. But I look forward to using them again once the Senedd approves them."

The Senedd declined to elaborate on the statement to MSs after being asked why the presiding officer's stance had changed.

Reform is currently holding an unrelated boycott of Senedd proceedings , after its member Joe Martin was barred from speaking by Irranca-Davies, after Martin claimed in parliament that white people were being "replaced" in the UK.

The smart glasses decision was issued to MSs before the presiding officer's ruling on Martin was issued .

stories.title: Youth scheme branded 'failure' over success rate
stories.summary: Under half of those on the youth schemes took up work, education or training in London, new data suggests.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training (Neet), according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics

Published 13 November 2026

Less than half of young people supported by two government-backed youth schemes in London went on to take up further education, employment or training (Neet) opportunities, according to new data.

Only 1,100 of 2,600 young Londoners supported by the £20m Youth Guarantee Trailblazer scheme moved into further opportunities.

Former youth worker and Conservative peer Shaun Bailey said the scheme was a "failure" and called for more support for employers but Skills Minister Jacqui Smith said it was helping young people furthest from the labour market and that it was still "early days".

A major report by former minister Alan Milburn is expected to set out proposals for tackling the problem next week .

Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training, according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics.

London is one of eight Youth Guarantee Trailblazer areas in England already exploring ways to help young Neets.

More than £20m in government funding is being spent on a variety of initiatives across London, from youth hubs to mental health support.

The money is funding two trailblazer projects in London, one focused on care-experienced young people in 12 boroughs, and a broader scheme that works across the capital.

The Greater London Authority (GLA), which leads the projects, has shared the initial results from year one of the two schemes with the BBC.

By the end of June 2026, London's two trailblazer schemes had offered support to more than 2,600 young people.

The programme offers a range of support, including access to mental health and wellbeing services at colleges and universities, help moving into further education, work experience, careers events, mentoring and practical help finding a job.

The programme is funded for two years until the end of March 2027.

'Constant rejections'

Mattie Davies is a 19-year-old from London.

He recently left college, and since then, has struggled to find work.

"I applied to a good few thousand and it's constant rejections," Davies said.

He has found work as a delivery driver but he says the wage is not enough to pay his bills.

"Uber will take anyone and that's what I didn't want," he said. "I wanted a job I could go into and break down all of my barriers and build myself up as a person."

He has not been receiving support from London's two Youth Guarantee Trailblazer schemes.

Instead, he's been getting support from Millwall FC, where he plays football, and its youth programmes.

Mattie Davies says applying for jobs has been a struggle

Lord Bailey said the government should instead focus on helping businesses employ young people.

"Sixty per cent of young people not moving into full-time employment or education show you it's actually a failure," Lord Bailey said.

"That money would be better spent giving businesses some headroom so that they can actually afford to employ young people."

The skills minister said London's Youth Guarantee Trailblazer schemes were helping young people who face several challenges, such as mental health difficulties or experience of the care system.

"The fact that a lot of them are succeeding at the first opportunity is a good result," the minister said.

"It's worked exactly in the terms we set for it, which is young people who were furthest away from the labour market able to get back into the labour market, and learning about how we engage with some of those young people."

The eight Youth Guarantee Trailblazers in England have received a total of £90m in central government funding over the two years of the programme.

The trailblazers were part of the Labour government's plan to help 16 to 24-year-olds classed as Neet, whose number has been rising in recent years.

There were 125,949 Neets in London at the end of 2025, the highest number of any region in England, according to government data.

stories.title: Young, Welsh and into politics - but with different views on independence
stories.summary: A body has been set up to consider the case for Welsh independence as well as more devolved powers.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Cerys and Patrick have different opinions on whether Wales should remain within the United Kingdom in the future

Published 12 November 2026

Cerys and Patrick have a lot in common. They're both young, Welsh, and very interested in politics.

The one thing they don't agree on is Wales' future within the United Kingdom.

A leading academic said the conversation around Welsh independence "has become normalised" amongst young people.

This week, the Plaid Cymru Welsh government set up a new body to consider the case for Welsh independence, as well as more devolution for Cardiff Bay.

For Patrick, he thinks his country is better off in the UK with more devolved powers, while Cerys believes an independent nation could offer more opportunities to people.

Nationalist party Plaid formed a government in Wales for the first after winning 46 seats during the May 2026 Senedd election .

While it hasn't called for a referendum on independence, the second line of its constitution says: "As the National Party of Wales, the party's aims shall be: to secure independence for Wales in Europe."

Pro-union party Reform UK is the second biggest in the Senedd after winning 34 seats in May's election.

Its Welsh leader Helen Jenner said voters "do not want to see Wales ripped out of the United Kingdom" and said the commission was "ridiculous".

This video can not be played

Young, Welsh and torn on independence

A recent poll by Survation for the pro-independence group YesCymru suggested people under 35 in Wales were more in favour of independence than their older peers.

"People feel left behind, especially my age," said Patrick, a 20-year-old student from Newport.

He added that he could understand why people were "energised and enthusiastic" about independence because of issues such as "student loans, the cost of living, the geopolitical scene".

But he said: "As of right now, I just do not think there is a case for it."

However, Patrick, said he would support further devolved powers for Wales within the union.

He said that "practical elements" such as whether there would be a border between Wales and England remain unanswered questions for him.

In Case You Misssed It - Young, political and torn on the future of the UK

12 November 2026

Are younger Welsh voters driving a shift towards independence? We examine why support is rising among under-35s, hear arguments from both sides and ask what the political future of Wales looks like.

For Cerys, learning to speak Welsh as an adult and broadening her understanding of history led to a "realisation" that Wales "in reality deserved a lot better than we had been given in the past and in the present".

"I think if we were independent, we could offer people more opportunity here," said the 35-year-old from Bridgend.

She added she'd like Wales to have further powers over policing and justice - a policy area currently controlled by Westminster.

"People seem to be kind of dangling the carrot of more devolution and never actually giving it to us," she said.

"More powers would be great but I will believe in those powers when I see them and until then, I think our best option is independence."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously said he was open to the idea of giving the Welsh government control of policing in Wales.

Cerys recently spoke at an independence rally in Aberystwyth alongside Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth

A leading academic from Cardiff University said "it's staggeringly important" that "young people are a majority in favour of independence".

"They see nothing strange or impossible about Wales becoming independent in the future," said Prof Laura McAllister, from the Welsh Governance Centre.

She said that there was "great scepticism" around the topic when you look at the opinions of people aged over 65, adding there was a "real demographic schism".

"There's going to need to be something much closer to support at least half the population supporting independence before there is any chance of a referendum being won," McAllister believes.

She added nobody "can afford to be complacent about the future of the union" because "the concept of the United Kingdom has no God-given right to survive in its current form".

"What we've seen in politics in recent times is that the potential for change is intrinsic to everything that happened," she said.

In 2024, McAllister co-chaired a commission which concluded Wales leaving the United Kingdom is a "viable" option .

Independence is one of the options being considered

With polling suggesting between 20% to 30% of people in Wales would be in favour of independence , external , academics have compared the current situation to Scotland in the years leading up to the independence referendum in 2014 .

"In some ways the situation here looks similar to Scotland in 2007," said Dr Jac Larner, a pollster and political analyst from Cardiff University, reflecting on when the Scottish National Party [SNP] took power.

"You might think now we have a party like Plaid Cymru, there's this inevitable march to this endless 50-50 that you see in Scotland, right?

"What's different here [in Wales] is that we still have a lot more hostility to the idea of devolution.

"You have about a third who want to get rid of the devolution altogether, maybe just less than a third who want independence."

Dr Jac Larner said attitudes towards independence and devolution are often driven by national identity

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said: "I have a vision for Wales, I support an independent Wales."

He said it was about "improving a lot of the people of Wales, tackling injustices, tackling unfairness, tackling inequalities, creating prosperity".

He added: "In the here and now, I deal with those issues dealing with the UK prime minister."

In October, the first ministers of Wales and Scotland met with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Glasgow for the National Economic Council , where devolution and funding were discussed.

Ap Iorwerth said there was "a new understanding of the injustice of rail expenditure in Wales" from Burnham, as well as "a realisation that this hasn't been given enough attention politically by UK governments in the past".

Following the 2026 Autumn Budget , ap Iorwerth told BBC Wales there were " paltry sums of money coming on rail , when they've said there's £14bn on the way" and a "real terms cut in the money we have to spend on public services".

A UK government spokesman said: "The prime minister passionately believes in our union and is optimistic about the future of the United Kingdom.

"Our position on referendums is clear - the prime minister is focused on practical solutions to help people with the cost of living and make a positive difference in people's everyday lives, not constitutional questions.

"Through the convening power of No10 North , the prime minister will build a constructive working relationship with each devolved government to explore how we can together contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."

stories.summary: Going undercover to expose an elaborate fraud aimed at obtaining fast-track settlement for wealthy migrants.

Watch: BBC undercover reporter is offered fake art and awards for 'talent' visa

Published 13 November 2026

Companies are offering to help migrants pose as talented artists and tech experts to make fraudulent UK visa applications under a fast-track immigration scheme, the BBC has found.

The UK government's Global Talent visa was launched in 2020 to attract the "brightest and best" scientists and researchers from around the world. It is also open to creative artists.

Following our investigation, the Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers, because it believes they were obtained by deception.

Applicants for Global Talent visas are not interviewed. People granted them need to prove they are exceptionally talented or promising in their field. They can then bring their families to the UK and there is a potentially quick path to permanent residency - in three or five years.

We have discovered that wealthy migrants looking to cheat the system are being offered fake art portfolios which they can pass off as their own work for a large fee.

A consultant from one company in London told our undercover reporter - who was posing as a potential client - that his firm could supply artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation.

No clients taking the "fully inclusive" package - costing more than £100,000 - had ever been refused a Global Talent visa, he said.

In the case of the two Nigerian men, our investigation was alerted to apparently faked newspaper articles reviewing their artistic work.

A well-known Nigerian art critic told us her name had been attached to online reviews praising the work of the two seemingly obscure artists.

"There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists," said Molara Wood.

Art critic Molara Wood told us her byline was added to online articles she had not written

Another woman we spoke to, who tried to get a talent visa via the tech route from India, told us a company she had used fabricated evidence for her application - including a made-up mentoring award and material falsely suggesting she had been a speaker at an event. Her application was rejected.

The Home Office described the findings of our investigation as "extremely serious" and said the company offering the £100,000 package to our reporter was already under investigation.

A spokesperson said they "will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system".

They added that the Global Talent route was already under review and "the home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused".

'It doesn't matter whether you're an artist'

The man who told us artwork could be created in China for clients said he was from a company called iCareer Consultancy UK, based in Canary Wharf. That is also where its sister company, ADArt Global Ltd, which is registered with the government regulator to offer immigration advice, is based.

Social media posts by iCareer employees pitch Global Talent visas as a route for wealthy Chinese nationals to come to the UK, without the need to speak English.

Our Global Talent visa service has "guaranteed approval", Peter told followers on social media

During a phone call and subsequent meeting with our undercover reporter, who spoke in Mandarin, the iCareer consultant told us:

At least four of his clients had obtained a Global Talent visa this year - and he suggested he currently had 10 people in the process of applying

The company could supply an employee to pose as a client and network at gallery openings - to help build evidence for a visa application

For an extra £28,000 the reporter could win a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine, also to help bolster an application

iCareer denied selling visa services and claimed the consultant had left its employment before he spoke to the undercover reporter - despite continuing to be listed on the company's website and providing us with a contract with the company's name and contact email address.

We began investigating iCareer after receiving a tip-off about its activities in the aftermath of our first investigation into fraudulent asylum claims , when we exposed how law firms and advisers were helping migrants pretend to be gay to obtain asylum.

The company, founded in 2018, is based in a co-working office and advertises itself as providing job search and careers coaching.

A consultant, who gave his name as Peter, had posted multiple times on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohonshu.

In one post from February this year, he boasted: "It doesn't actually matter whether you're an artist… Our Global Talent visa service in the arts is fully inclusive, with guaranteed approval… We say we can do it even if you aren't an artist, because we include the artworks as well."

An ADArt brochure is filled with photos of art galleries

In another video, Peter - whose real name is Shilong Guan - said he recommended the Global Talent visa in the arts because every other route to UK settlement had an "extremely high English language requirement".

Included in his posts on another social media platform, under the username "iCareerPeter", were redacted names of people whose applications had been approved, he said.

While we could not clarify Peter's claims, a senior immigration lawyer, Harjap Singh Bhangal, who reviewed all our findings, said helping people pose as artists in this way amounted to a "sophisticated fraud".

The whole purpose "is to attempt to defraud the Home Office and convince them, and an endorser, that I'm a genuine person, a genuine artist," he explained.

Although introduced by the Conservatives, Global Talent visas have been enthusiastically championed by the current Labour government - even as it toughens rules elsewhere to try to reduce net migration.

About 6,600 were granted in 2025, with applications in the arts and culture category nearly doubling between 2023 and 2025.

Applications must be approved by the relevant body, which for arts and culture applications is Arts Council England. It endorsed just under half of the nearly 3,500 applications it received last year.

The only way around this is if applicants have won a major award. In the film and TV sector, for example, the award must be an Oscar, Bafta or Golden Globe in one of the main categories.

Arts Council England told us it took allegations of fraud seriously and investigated where evidence was "suggested to have been misleading or fraudulent".

We would be provided with up to 15 pieces of evidence, stated the contract we were sent

Peter told our undercover reporter it was not a problem if she had no background in art and could not speak English. He could help her get a visa for artists who show "exceptional promise", he said.

"We would handle the production of all your artworks," he explained, adding it was cheaper to commission artists in China than in the UK.

Our reporter would get up to 15 works and have to pay about 10,000 yuan (£1,120) postage to get the works from Beijing to London.

Fine art options included oil paintings, illustration, sculpture, installation, digital art and photography, he explained.

To help her application, Peter said iCareer would arrange exhibitions and media coverage critiquing the reporter's work. Some information would be backdated to make it look like she had been an artist for some time.

During the call, and a subsequent face-to-face meeting, Peter also outlined how he could help our reporter win a prestigious award for Chinese artists - sponsored by American media company, Forbes.

Our contract also stated we would get help winning a Forbes-sponsored award

Being a winner in the Forbes China Future Artists Awards would help her visa application, he said, but the additional fee would be about 250,000 yuan (£28,000). Money would be refunded if she did not win.

The BBC approached Forbes for comment and it confirmed to us that the awards are genuine and that ADArt, iCareer Consultancy's sister company, is a sponsor.

It said the judging process is based on the "high standards of Forbes globally" and handled by the Forbes China editorial team, with assistance from professional judges.

Also as part of the visa deception, our reporter would have to do some "work experience… online or in person", said Peter. The reporter asked how she could do this, given she could not speak English.

This was no problem, he responded - one of his colleagues could do it, and also pose as her at gallery openings, to network on her behalf.

Officials administering the visas "don't look at photographs" said Peter.

The whole process would take at least two years, he explained, meaning her application would not be ready until the end of 2028 or early 2029.

The price for the "fully inclusive" visa service would be 880,000 yuan (about £98,000) paid in three stages - with an additional 20% VAT due if our reporter chose to pay in sterling.

The BBC was sent "a contract to break the law", according to immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal

During the call, Peter sent over a contract setting out how iCareer would provide "necessary endorsement materials" for a visa application.

The reporter asked if there was any possibility the application wouldn't pass.

"There's no such possibility," Peter replied. "We keep working for you until we get the result."

He added that the reporter would be refunded if her application failed because of material provided by iCareer.

Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal said Peter had sent us "a contract to break the law".

When we called Peter to confront him about the claims he had made to our undercover reporter, he denied he was willing to help people pretend to be artists or have artwork made.

"We are not doing anything wrong or illegal, all of our artists are real artists," he told us.

iCareer, via lawyers, subsequently said that Peter's employment had ended in early October, shortly before he spoke to the undercover reporter - adding that the company strongly denied "offering any visa services whatsoever".

"The meeting described by the BBC was not authorised by iCareer," it said. "We do not endorse the representations or purported services attributed to him."

The company added it had been unaware that Peter and another employee had made social media posts promoting these services and would investigate.

It said that ADArt, which has the same owner as iCareer and was described by Peter to the undercover reporter as another division within the iCareer group, "signs artists and helps them curate exhibitions and develop professional relationships".

Peter continued to be listed as an employee on iCareer's website, and on his own LinkedIn profile, until the company was contacted by the BBC, which iCareer described as an oversight.

Our undercover meeting with him took place in the same Canary Wharf building where iCareer and ADArt are based, a co-working space. He also provided us with an iCareer brochure and sent a contract with a corporate iCareer email contact address.

Two visas revoked

Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal says he has no doubt that some fraudulent claims will get through.

We have learned that the two Nigerian men purporting to be fine art photographers - whose visas have now been revoked because of our investigation - successfully obtained talent visas on the basis of faked evidence.

Their deception first came to light when art critic Molara Wood discovered articles reviewing their work in the Nigerian Tribune - which were under her byline despite the fact she had not written them.

The articles were taken down after she alerted the paper's editors.

The Tribune told us it had identified a "staff member who had posted the articles on our website without authorisation".

It said the employee admitted that "an individual outside the organisation had supplied the articles" but that he had denied being paid for it.

Wood said the criticism attributed to her was of poor quality, as were the artworks.

"It is writing that I would not want associated with me," says Wood. "The images were not worthy of comment."

Part of the article, including artwork purporting to be by Silva Ndifon, that Molara Wood did not write

Other critics have also had the same thing happen to them, she says.

Artists applying for the Global Talent visa have to provide at least two examples of recent press coverage reviewing or profiling their work.

The two men who were supposedly reviewed by Wood - Silva Ndifon and Adanu Emmanuel Okoko - are now thought to be living in the UK.

While one of them does boast an online portfolio, it does not feature the kind of fine-art photography described in the article that Wood did not write. The other appears to have little to connect him to photography, or any other kind of art, beyond the article Wood found.

Neither responded to the BBC's requests for comment. After the Home Office was contacted by the BBC, it is now understood their visas are in the process of being revoked.

Cider maker Matilda Temperley said the budget had been "disappointing"

Published 13 November 2026

Rising costs could force the cider industry to reduce their reliance on British-grown apples, according to several well-established businesses.

Higher alcohol duty, energy bills and packaging costs are making it harder to stay profitable, according to a producer in Somerset.

The government said it was supporting the sector by increasing the value of Small Producer Relief, which provides lower alcohol duty rates for some smaller and medium-sized producers.

Matilda Temperley, director of Burrow Hill farm near Martock, said it would be a "tragedy" to stop using its own apples due to climbing costs.

Temperley, whose farm has been growing apples for 300 years, said recent increases had added to pressures already facing the industry, adding at 6% alcohol, their traditional cider is taxed at a higher rate than mass produced cider.

More from Somerset

Christmas market fears as roadworks cause long delays Published 2 days ago

Gritters out for the first time this autumn Published 2 days ago

No radical change after nationalisation, GWR says Published 2 days ago

"By next February, we will have seen a 61% increase in tax on our standard 50cl bottles," Temperley claimed.

She welcomed the rise in Small Producers Relief but said other mounting costs outweighed it.

"We've got huge, energy costs, then almost a 90% increase in tax costs since 2020."

"The thing that will happen is that if you're a big cider maker, you're going to look to cut your costs and the only way to cut costs is to stop using British apples," she said.

"That's a real tragedy because cider should be made from these beautiful orchards".

Isaac Stell says ultimately it will be the consumer who pays

Isaac Stell, a financial analyst at Wealth Club in Bristol, said that having pledged not to raise the main rates of income tax, national insurance or VAT for working people, the recent budget focused on other areas to "help plug the fiscal hole."

He said producers were also dealing with higher employer National Insurance contributions and increases in the minimum wage.

"Inevitably, some of those additional costs will find their way through to the pubs, clubs and restaurants that producers supply, and ultimately to an already squeezed consumer. "

Matthew Showering said like his apples - his business is growing

The Showerings family, known for producing Babycham, has been making drinks in Shepton Mallet for more than 14 generations.

"Our business has grown a lot in the last ten years - we've gone from having 80 employees to around 350 now," the firm's managing director Matthew Showering said.

"We've had a good couple of years, we're making drinks that are popular and growing."

While acknowledging rising costs, Showering said he would rather see less government intervention.

"We don't want any help from the government, we'd rather they keep out of things as much as possible."

Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider with his apple picker Johnny

Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider in Low Ham said the size of his operation means he will be eligible for the Small Producer Relief but adds he will not see a huge benefit as the Alcohol Duty is a "fairly substantial" part of his monthly outgoings.

Gillett remains optimistic, and said he would not consider importing pulp or concentrate to cut costs.

"We are a craft producer here in Somerset and are proud of the fact we take from local orchards, traditional orchards, and use the fruit that is available here in this county."

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The cider industry makes a vital contribution to our rural economy and communities, and cider continues to benefit from significantly lower duty rates than other alcoholic drinks.

"But we know the industry is facing continued pressures, which is why the Budget provides additional support by cutting costs for pubs and bars that are vital customers for the industry and poured pints continue to benefit from draught relief."
